items.title: The chain rule explains why a car's acceleration depends on both gear and rpm
items.claim: A car's speed (v) depends on engine rpm (omega) through the gear ratio. Engine rpm depends on time as the driver presses the throttle. The chain rule says dv/dt = (dv/d(omega)) * (d(omega)/dt). Acceleration is the product of two derivatives.
items.prompt: What's the chain rule's geometric meaning?

options.text: When y depends on u and u depends on t, a small change in t produces a small change in u (scaled by du/dt) which produces a small change in y (scaled by dy/du); chaining the scalings gives dy/dt = (dy/du)(du/dt)
It is wrong for vector quantities

items.reveal_title: The chain rule as composition of rates
items.reveal:
If y = f(u) and u = g(t), then y = f(g(t)). The chain rule: dy/dt = f'(g(t)) * g'(t) = (dy/du) * (du/dt).

Geometric intuition: a small Delta t produces a small Delta u (approximately (du/dt) * Delta t), which produces a small Delta y (approximately (dy/du) * Delta u). Combining: Delta y ≈ (dy/du)(du/dt) Delta t. Take the limit and you get the chain rule.

Physics examples:
- A particle's position depends on time. Its velocity depends on its position (e.g., in a velocity field). Acceleration = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v dv/dx. This is the Eulerian-Lagrangian connection in fluid mechanics.
- Optics: refractive index varies with position. The ray equation involves chain rules through the index.
- Thermodynamics: pressure depends on temperature and volume. Derivatives form a web of chain rules — Maxwell relations.

The chain rule is the BACKBONE of backpropagation in neural networks: gradients of a loss with respect to weights are computed via chain rules through layers of the network. Training deep neural networks is essentially repeated chain rule applications across millions of parameters.

When u or g has multiple components (vector-valued), the chain rule becomes the JACOBIAN rule — products of matrices of partial derivatives.
items.why: The chain rule looks like a notational identity. It's the fundamental principle of compositional change — appearing in physics, optimisation, neural networks, and any setting where one variable depends on another through an intermediate.

items.title: A shape with finite volume but infinite surface area
items.claim: Rotate y = 1/x for x at least 1 around the x-axis. You get a 'horn' extending to infinity. Its volume is exactly pi (finite). Its surface area is infinite. You could fill it with paint, but never paint its interior.
items.prompt: How can volume be finite if surface area isn't?

options.text: The horn cannot be constructed in reality
Volume integrates 1/x squared (which is summable), while surface integrates 1/x (which is not); the integrals are independent, and one can converge while the other diverges
Surface and volume are always proportional in finite shapes

items.reveal:
Volume: V = pi * integral from 1 to infinity of (1/x) squared dx = pi * [-1/x] from 1 to infinity = pi.

Surface area: A = 2 * pi * integral from 1 to infinity of (1/x) * sqrt(1 + 1/x to the fourth) dx, which is greater than 2 * pi * integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x = infinity.

Intuition: volume scales as the square of the radius, surface as the radius. As you stretch toward infinity, the cross-sectional radius decreases as 1/x — the square (volume per unit length) decreases as 1/x squared (summable), but the radius itself (surface per unit length) decreases as 1/x (the harmonic series, divergent).

The 'paint paradox': filling the horn with pi cubic units of paint coats the interior — even though the surface 'should' need infinite paint to cover. The resolution: a paint film of any finite thickness doesn't fit at the horn's far reaches, where the radius is arbitrarily small.
items.why: Geometric intuition equates surface area and volume scaling. They're separate integrals; convergence of one doesn't imply convergence of the other.

items.title: 45 degrees is only optimal for a projectile in a vacuum
items.claim: Every physics textbook says the maximum range for a projectile is at launch angle 45 degrees. True in vacuum. In real air, the optimum angle is significantly less — and for some launches it's barely above 30 degrees.
items.prompt: Why does air change the optimum?

options.text: It doesn't — 45 degrees is always optimal
Air resistance reduces both horizontal velocity and vertical velocity, but the loss to drag is greater on long airborne paths; lowering the angle reduces flight time and total drag exposure
Gravity is different at high angles

items.reveal:
Vacuum case: range = (v^2 / g) * sin(2 * theta). Maximised at theta = 45 degrees.

With linear drag (low-speed air): the optimum angle decreases with launch speed and drag coefficient. For a thrown baseball or shot put, optimum is ~42-43 degrees.

With quadratic drag (more realistic at high speed): for a golf ball, optimum is closer to 12-15 degrees (combined with backspin for lift). For an artillery shell, often 30-40 degrees due to high muzzle velocity and dense air.

Why: higher launch angles mean longer flight times, more time exposed to drag, more total energy lost. The trade-off between vertical reach and drag loss shifts the optimum downward.

For a long-jumper, who launches around 7-10 m/s, the optimum angle calculated from biomechanics is ~22 degrees, not 45 — because the long-jumper cannot achieve high vertical velocity from horizontal sprint and because air resistance is minor. Body-mechanics constraints matter more than the equation.

The 45° result is a useful first approximation but should not be taken as universal. Most real-world projectile design uses computational fluid dynamics rather than analytical formulas.
items.why: Textbook results assume ideal conditions. In real applications (golf, baseball, artillery, athletics), the answer is shifted — often substantially — by drag and biomechanical constraints. 'Theoretically 45°' is correct for nothing on Earth.
